facts.value: Treasury & Prudential Indicator Management: Quarter 4 (to 31 March 2026), for Cabinet on 25 June 2026 (CAB/25). Ten-page narrative report on the investment side of a debt-free district. Appendix A (Investment Limits), Appendix B (Investments as at 31 March 2026) and Appendix C (Prudential Indicators and Treasury Management Targets) are referenced throughout but NOT bound into the 10-page PDF and NOT held on disk. Appendix J attached under s83760 is the Write Off/Excusal of Debt Summary — a Revenue Management report appendix, not part of this treasury paper. Adviser: MUFG Corporate Markets. Report Author Clare Hazard, Accountancy Manager. Lead Director Lee Colyer, Director of Finance, Policy & Development.

source.title: Treasury and Prudential Indicator Management Report Quarter 4 (to 31 March 2026) — Cabinet, 25 June 2026

facts.note: The 10-page PDF ends at §8 Cross-Cutting Issues on p.10 and does not carry the appendices it references. That is a significant coverage gap for a treasury paper: everything about the split of investments by counterparty, the maturity profile, the CFR, the external debt figure and the prudential indicator numerics lives in appendices we do not hold. The reconcilable content in this paper is the investment income line and the average rate on the portfolio — nothing about borrowing, and nothing that lets us test the balance-sheet identity.

facts.value: Opening cash balance 1 April 2025: £47.7m (§2.8). Closing cash balance 31 March 2026: £41.916m of investments and bank account money (§2.4 and §2.11). 2025/26 budget was set on average funds available of £41.5m (§2.7). Equated Investments across the year came in at £59.834m Q4 actual (vs £41.5m budget and £59.5m Q3 forecast) — average portfolio £18.334m higher than planned (§2.14).
facts.note: The gap between opening (£47.7m) and closing (£41.916m) is a £5.784m draw on cash across the year — but funds available for investment across the year averaged £59.834m, well above closing, because grants and receipts were held mid-year before being paid out. The 'equated' basis is the through-the-year average used to compute the interest budget, which is why it is the number the £2.738m interest gets divided against for the 4.58% headline rate.

facts.value: Investment and bank interest actual 2025/26: £2,738,000 against £2,000,000 budget — £738,000 surplus (§2.13). Q3 forecast had been £2,720,000, so a further £18,000 came in through Q4. Portfolio weighted-average interest rate 4.58% (§2.15). Target rate had been 4.82% at strategy-setting (§2.12). Other Interest and Investment Income: £69,288 actual against £48,800 budget — £20,488 surplus (Property Income £45,000, Mortgage Interest £2,034, Other Interest £22,254 — §2.20). Total treasury income £2,807,288 against combined budget £2,048,800 — £758,488 surplus. Prudential Indicators not breached during the quarter (§2.18) — detail lives in Appendix C which we do not hold.
facts.note: The 4.58% weighted-average is 24bp below the 4.82% target — but the target was set into a 4.50% Bank Rate that then fell 75bp across the year to 3.75%. So the portfolio outperformed the base-rate trajectory comfortably: 83bp above closing Bank Rate at year-end. The paper's own §2.15 explains this — 'the Council had placed some longer-term investments whilst interest rates were at their peak', so the term-out decision is what carried the yield when new money went in at lower rates. This is a demonstrable good call in the paper's own words.

facts.value: Bank Rate 4.50% at year start; three 25bp cuts (May 2025, August 2025, December 2025) took it to 3.75% by year-end. MPC held at 3.75% in February and March 2026. MPC also held at 3.75% at its 30 April 2026 meeting. MUFG (adviser) had previously forecast further cuts through 2026 but revised post-US/Israel-Iran conflict view is Bank Rate held at 3.75% until September 2027 (§2.5-2.6).
facts.note: MUFG's post-March central case (Bank Rate held to September 2027) is a longer flat forecast than most council advisers were publishing this cycle. Arlingclose-advised councils in the same batch (Newcastle-under-Lyme, several others) print a similar hold view; MUFG is the same shape but the flat period runs further. This is an adviser view printed in a council paper, not our own view, so it can be reflected back.

facts.value: Cash held above the budget-setting expectation because of capital rescheduling and revenue underspends: £11.178m of capital projects were rescheduled out of 2024/25 into 2025/26 (§2.9); a further £8.859m of capital was rescheduled during Q1-Q3 25/26 into future years, with an additional £5.215m rescheduled in Q4 25/26 (§2.10) — total £14.074m pushed out during the year on top of what came in from the prior year. £10.276m of unspent Section 106 monies held at year-end (§2.10). Revenue net expenditure 2025/26 came in £1,624,000 under budget (§2.10); 2024/25 net expenditure had also come in £0.910m under budget (§2.9), both flowing to reserves.
facts.note: £14.074m rescheduled OUT of 25/26 during the year is a material capital slippage — but this is a treasury paper, so the finding is about what it did to the cash pile, not about capital delivery. The paper is explicit that the surplus cash will need to be used in future years to fund the capital programme (§2.10), so this is timing not a permanent windfall. That matters for the email tone: we don't want to imply the £738k represents 'free money' when the paper says otherwise.

facts.value: The £738,000 investment interest surplus will be transferred to reserves: £688,000 to the Capital and Revenue Initiatives Reserve (to fund the capital programme) and £50,000 to the Local Government Reorganisation Reserve (to fund future LGR costs) (§2.16). The £20,488 other-interest surplus will also go to the Capital and Revenue Initiatives Reserve (§2.21). The Council 'has returned to its policy of any interest achieved that is surplus to budget, being transferred to reserves. This policy protects the Council from building short term interest windfalls into its base budget' (§2.16 verbatim).
facts.note: Two things worth noting for internal reference. First, the explicit policy — surplus interest to reserves rather than into the base — is a discipline that many councils don't spell out. Second, the £50k transfer to the 'Local Government Reorganisation Reserve' is a real line item: Kent LGR is an active workstream and Tunbridge Wells Borough Council is one of the districts inside the county reorganisation. The LGR angle is not something to raise in an outreach email (it edges into 'you may cease to exist' territory) but the paper itself flags a reserve for it.

facts.value: No PWLB borrower record for Tunbridge Wells in price_book.py. Confirmed via price_book.py --find 'Tunbridge Wells' (no match), --find 'Tunbridge' (no match), --find 'Wells' (only WELLS CITY COUNCIL (SOMERSET) and BUILTH WELLS TOWN COUNCIL (POWYS), both unrelated). The paper itself carries no external borrowing figure, no CFR, no maturity profile of debt, and no reference to PWLB at any point across its 10 pages — consistent with a debt-free district running an investment-only treasury operation. Our zero holding is the position both sides are on.

source.title: PWLBtoday borrower search (price_book.py) against paper (silence on borrowing)

facts.note: This is the reconciliation for a council with no PWLB debt: absence on both sides. The paper's silence on borrowing is not itself proof of a debt-free position (a debt figure could sit in the missing Appendix C prudential indicator table), but the absence of any narrative reference to borrowing in the 10-page report, combined with an empty price_book, is strongly consistent with a council that has no PWLB debt. Recorded as an absence-tie, same pattern as Newcastle-under-Lyme.

facts.value: CANNOT be tested from this paper. The identity CFR − external borrowing − other long-term liabilities = internal borrowing requires the CFR figure, which lives in Appendix C (Prudential Indicators). Appendix C is referenced at §2.17 but is NOT bound into the 10-page PDF held on disk and is NOT held separately. Consequently the balance-sheet identity is recorded as unverified in this note — not as failed, and not as ties. The paper carries no CFR figure, no external borrowing figure and no other-long-term-liabilities figure anywhere in its narrative.

source.title: §2.17 — p.6 (paper references Appendix C but it is not in the document held)

facts.note: The email should reflect this coverage gap plainly rather than gloss it. We can say we've read the Q4 treasury paper; we cannot say we've reconciled the balance sheet, because the underlying numbers are in an appendix we do not hold. This is a genuine limitation and hiding it would be exactly the kind of thing that ends a first contact.

officer.body:
Dear [RECIPIENT NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a couple of thoughts on your Q4 Treasury and Prudential Indicator Management report that Cabinet received on 25 June. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your report is short and clean, which we say plainly because most of what we read isn't, and this is offered in that spirit rather than as a critique.

Upfront, so we're clear about scope. We hold no PWLB loans for the Council in our book, and your report doesn't reference any external borrowing across its ten pages, so both sides are on the same position: no PWLB debt to reconcile. We should also flag that the Appendix C prudential indicator table you reference at 2.17 isn't bound into the PDF that's published under s83736 — so we're commenting on the narrative, not on the underlying CFR or borrowing indicators. That limits what we can responsibly say, and it's better to name that at the top than have you notice.

The thing worth writing about is the sentence at your 2.15. You describe the 4.58% year-average as 'under target' at 2.19, because the strategy was written to 4.82%. But the target was set into a 4.50% Bank Rate that then fell 75 basis points across the year to 3.75% by December, and against that trajectory 4.58% is a meaningful outperformance of where the base rate went. Your own 2.15 explains why: some longer-term investments were placed 'whilst interest rates were at their peak', and it's those that held the portfolio yield up when the new money went in at lower rates. Read that way, the paper is describing a term-out call that worked — and one it's easy to underplay because the target number is what it's measured against. Where we can help is with the reference frame around it. Our monthly page at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity carries the actual PWLB draws the sector took each month at both fixings (July: £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers, average 5.02% on certainty), which is the closest thing to a national reference point for what money was actually costing councils through the year.

On the forecast, MUFG's central view at your 2.6 is Bank Rate held at 3.75% until September 2027. That's a longer flat period than most council advisers have printed this cycle. It's their view in your paper, not ours to argue with, but it does shape the question of when the next term-deposit decision looks attractive and against what curve. That's the kind of thing our daily SONIA path and rate history pages are built to sit alongside — take a look at pwlbtoday.org for the front page.

On training, three courses fit the paper. PWLB rates — reading the curve is the natural companion to your 2.5 and 2.6. Short-term liquidity and the LA-to-LA market fits where the year's excess cash was placed. And the Liability benchmark pathway is worth a look given CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates will put it in front of every S151 — it's a lighter fit for a debt-free district than for a heavy borrower, but the framework matters ahead of any future capital-financing decision. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts are open to the whole team.

If any of this turns out to be useful, mentioning it to colleagues or neighbours would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
